prompt: Review the cache-tier inputs in `fixture/` and choose a production configuration from the candidate list. Write the architecture decision record to `docs/adr/0001-cache.md`. Explain the selected topology, sizing arithmetic, availability behavior, cost, and why the other serious option was not selected. The ADR must contain a fenced block whose info string is exactly `decision`; its JSON must have exactly the keys `chosen`, `options`, `limits`, and `monthly_cost_usd`. Set `chosen` to the selected option id, `options` to the option ids considered, `limits` to an object mapping each hard-limit name to `{"limit": number, "value": number}`, and `monthly_cost_usd` to the selected option's monthly cost computed from the price sheet. Include one limits entry for every hard limit in the inputs, with the chosen configuration's computed value and the input limit number.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ln -sfn . solution && node --require ./hidden/gate.js --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: The ADR explains the sizing arithmetic, including the engine reservation, primary versus replica capacity, and why the selected topology meets the peak working set and availability objectives. Fail: sizes nodes by advertised memory, or assumes the replica adds capacity. Partial: applies the 25% reservation but misses that replicas give failover, not primary capacity, or compares to the wrong working set. Pass: shows minimal-105 gives 105 x 0.75 = 78.75 GB primary (about 66.7% of the 118 GB peak, failing the 95% in-memory floor) while balanced-105 gives 157.5 GB across two primaries, explains replicas add no capacity but give 0-minute RPO and about 3-minute RTO against the 5-minute limit, and uses the 800 requests/s production target, not the superseded 600. (not code-checkable: Tests can recompute reported figures but cannot judge whether the explanation connects the figures into a sound architectural argument.)

The ADR compares the selected option with a viable alternative and makes a clear cost, capacity, performance, and operational tradeoff rather than asserting a choice. Fail: lists options with no comparison, or picks on price only. Partial: compares balanced-105 and wide-209 on cost only. Pass: compares balanced-105 (4 x 650 = 2,600 USD, two primary shards) with wide-209 (2 x 1,400 = 2,800 USD, one shard, lower p95, fewer nodes) on at least two of cost, shard layout, latency and operations, states the 200 USD per month difference, and says what would change the decision (118 GB peak growing past 157.5 GB, or spend nearing the 3,000 USD budget). (not code-checkable: Tests can verify option ids and numeric limits but cannot assess whether the comparison is meaningful or the preference is well justified.)

The record rejects each option it did not choose for a reason taken from the fixture (a limit, a cost, a requirement or a measurement), and states the consequence of the chosen option the team must live with. Fail: names the winner only, or rejects options for generic reasons ("too complex", "not scalable") the fixture does not support. Partial: most rejected options get a fixture-based reason, but one is waved away or the cost of the chosen option is not stated. Pass: every rejected option has a reason quoted or computed from the fixture, the chosen option's main downside is stated, and the record says what would change the decision. (code cannot check this because tests check the chosen id and the numbers, not whether each rejection is grounded)

verdicts.note: The prompt asks to choose from candidate list and write an ADR without naming methods, frameworks, or revealing which option is correct.
All limits are clearly specified with numeric values and units; the calculation methodology (engine reservation, primary vs replica) is documented in the operating model.
The fixture provides inputs but does not state which candidate to choose; the agent must derive the correct answer by computing limit compliance.
The task requires multi-file synthesis and arithmetic (memory reservation, shard multiplication, cost calculation); picking the cheapest option fails the hit-ratio limit.
All necessary numbers are present: peak working set, throughput target, node specs, prices, reservation percentage, and service limits are fully specified.

items.note: task.json:3 specifies the deliverable, input interfaces, and exact output schema, but does not prescribe a method, tool, checklist, or specific choice or trap.
fixture/README.md:3-7 and the input files provide source facts and constraints, not a prewritten decision or list of findings; the candidate choice and computed values still require reasoning.

fixture/candidate-configs.json:4-22, traffic-profile.md:8-11, operating-model.md:3-13, service-requirements.md:7-13, node-benchmarks.csv:2-4, and price-sheet.json:5-7 support the expected options, limits, arithmetic, availability, and tradeoffs.

The fixture contains all required topology, memory-reservation, peak-demand, benchmark, price, and service-objective inputs; the calculations and acceptable candidates follow directly from those files.

items.text: States that the 600 requests/second staging pilot value is superseded by the 800 requests/second production target and must not be used for capacity planning.

items.text: Computes that minimal-105's single primary node provides only 78.75 GB after the 25% engine reservation (105 × 0.75), which covers approximately 66.7% of the 118 GB peak working set and therefore fails the 95% in-memory hit-ratio floor.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: Clarifies that replicas provide failover availability and do not add to primary working-set capacity, so the minimal-105 replica does not compensate for insufficient primary memory.
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Verifies monthly cost by multiplying node count by per-node price from the price sheet: balanced-105 costs 4 × 650 = 2,600 USD/month; wide-209 costs 2 × 1,400 = 2,800 USD/month.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: Compares balanced-105 and wide-209 on at least two trade-off dimensions: cost (balanced costs 200 USD/month less), shard topology (balanced has two primary shards vs one), latency (wide has lower p95 latency), or operational complexity (fewer nodes with wide).
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: States the availability behavior: a replica provides zero-minute RPO and approximately three-minute RTO under the operating model, meeting the service requirements of 0-minute RPO and 5-minute RTO.
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Notes what would change the decision: the 118 GB peak working set growing beyond the 157.5 GB usable primary memory, or the 2,600 USD monthly spend approaching the 3,000 USD budget limit.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

weakAnswers: Picks minimal-105 because it is the cheapest option with a replica, without computing whether its 78.75 GB primary capacity meets the 118 GB peak requirement.
Uses the staging pilot value of 600 requests/second instead of the 800 requests/second production target for throughput capacity planning.
Assumes the replica in minimal-105 doubles capacity to 157.5 GB, not understanding that replicas are for availability and do not serve primary working-set traffic.
Selects wide-209 solely because it has fewer nodes and lower latency, without comparing the 200 USD/month cost difference against the balanced option.
Lists the candidates without computing the engine reservation (25%) and its impact on usable memory for each topology.
